segments.t: Create ASCII art in three ways: render text as a FIGlet banner, let the AI draw a picture from a subject such as "house in the forest", or convert an existing image file. All three sit in one dialog behind their own tab, share a zoomable preview, and copy to the clipboard — plain, as a code comment, or as ready-made print statements — for use in terminal scripts, login banners, or documentation.

Open the dialog from KTPH006Tools KTPH020 ASCII Art...KTPH007 in the menu bar, or press KTPH008KTPH000KTPH009+KTPH010KTPH001KTPH011+KTPH012KTPH002KTPH013 (KTPH014KTPH003KTPH015+KTPH016KTPH004KTPH017+KTPH018KTPH005KTPH019 on macOS).

Choose a FIGlet font style from the dropdown. KTPH000StandardKTPH001 and KTPH002SlantKTPH003 come from the jfiglet library; KTPH0043-DKTPH005, KTPH006bannerKTPH007, KTPH008bigKTPH009, KTPH010blockKTPH011, KTPH012cosmicKTPH013, KTPH014DigitalKTPH015, KTPH016LeanKTPH017, KTPH018romanKTPH019, KTPH020scriptKTPH021 and KTPH022smallKTPH023 are bundled FIGfonts. A style whose font file cannot be loaded is left out of the list.

Switch between styles with the dropdown, with the arrow keys (KTPH004KTPH000KTPH005, KTPH006KTPH001KTPH007, KTPH008KTPH002KTPH009, KTPH010KTPH003KTPH011) while the dropdown has focus, or with the ◀ and ▶ buttons beside it.
Type or paste the text to convert into the KTPH000TextKTPH001 field. Multi-line input is supported — each line is converted on its own, and blank lines stay blank.
The KTPH000PreviewKTPH001 re-renders as you type and whenever you change the style.

Instead of lettering, this tab asks a model to draw the subject as a small vector drawing (a restricted SVG), which korTTY then converts into ASCII characters itself — a model is far better at describing shapes than at typing aligned characters.
The thing to draw, for example KTPH000. Pressing KTPH002KTPH001KTPH003 starts the generation.
The character grid the picture is fitted into: Small (40 × 20), Medium (60 × 30), Large (80 × 40) or Extra large (100 × 50). Remembered between sessions.
Requests a picture for the subject.
Which profile handles this run. The choice is transient and does not change your default profile.
Redraws the same subject with a different treatment — viewpoint, level of detail, scene context, geometric style, proportions, contrast or tones — asking for something different again on each retry.
Stops the running generation; the previous picture stays.
The tab needs at least one configured AI profile and the AI features switch enabled; otherwise its controls stay disabled and the status line says so.

The status line names the current step: asking the AI for a drawing, converting it to characters, asking once more, or asking the AI to type the picture directly. If an answer holds no usable drawing, korTTY asks once more and tells the model what was wrong; if that fails too, it falls back to asking the model to type the ASCII picture directly and says so in the status line. Errors, a cut-off answer and "no usable picture" replies are reported there as well, together with the reason.

The model returns a drawing rather than characters: korTTY draws it off-screen, fits it into the chosen size and picks one printable ASCII character per cell, so the result is always plain ASCII that fits the grid, with blank edge rows and columns trimmed. A drawing is checked before it is shown — it must contain shapes, lie inside its canvas, be neither blank nor one solid block, and be large enough. Only the direct-typing fallback shows the model's own characters, cleaned as before and cropped to the chosen size: a fenced code block is unwrapped, reasoning blocks and control characters are removed, tabs become spaces, and blank leading and trailing lines are trimmed. For this action korTTY switches the model's reasoning off where the profile allows it, caps the answer length and skips knowledge stores, because a picture gains nothing from either.

This tab converts an existing picture — a photo, a logo, an icon — into ASCII art on your machine; no AI profile is involved. Open a file with KTPH000Open image…KTPH001 or drop it onto the tab. PNG, JPEG, GIF and BMP are read.
The character grid the picture is fitted into, keeping its aspect ratio: a landscape photo uses fewer rows, a portrait one fewer columns. Remembered between sessions.
Shifts all tones lighter or darker.
Spreads or flattens the tones around mid grey.
Swaps light and dark. ASCII ink is dark on light, so a light subject on a dark background reads correctly only when inverted.
Returns brightness, contrast and inversion to neutral.
Every change converts again immediately, and the status line shows the source size in pixels and the result size in characters.

Before your adjustments apply, korTTY stretches the picture's own tonal range to full contrast (ignoring the darkest and lightest percent of pixels), because photos cluster in the mid tones and would otherwise become one grey block. Transparent pixels count as white paper. Very large files are reduced to 1600 pixels on the long edge when they are opened; more detail cannot reach the character grid anyway. Freestanding subjects, logos and icons convert well; busy photographs need a large size and usually some contrast.
All tabs share one zoom level, so a banner and a picture are always shown at the same size.
KTPH003+KTPH004 button, KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008, or KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 and scroll up over the preview
KTPH003−KTPH004 button, KTPH005KTPH000KTPH006+KTPH007KTPH001KTPH008, or KTPH009KTPH002KTPH010 and scroll down over the preview
The percentage between the buttons shows the current level, from 50 % to 333 %, where 100 % is the default 12 px monospace size.

KTPH000Copy to ClipboardKTPH001 copies the preview of the tab that is currently open, so you get the banner from the Text Banner tab and the picture from the AI Picture or Image File tab. The KTPH002Copy asKTPH003 row above the buttons decides the shape of what lands on the clipboard, so a picture can be pasted straight into program code:
Puts a comment marker in front of every picture line, or wraps the picture in a block comment, so it can sit inside source code without being executed.
Turns every picture line into a print statement of the chosen language, with the quoting and escaping that language needs, so a script prints the picture as-is.
The number of spaces placed before every picture line — between the comment marker and the picture, or inside the printed string — to align the picture. 0 to 20, default 1.

Comment and output code exclude each other: choosing one resets the other to KTPH000NoneKTPH001. All three choices are remembered between sessions, and the copy button's tooltip shows the first line as it will be copied.
Bash, Perl, Python, Ruby, YAML, TOML, PowerShell
Java, C, C++, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust, Kotlin, Swift, PHP
C-style block comment; every picture line is prefixed with KTPH000
JSON string array — the picture as a list of string values
KTPH000 … KTPH001 — no escaping at all

A few characters have to change so the copied text stays valid: inside a C-style block comment KTPH000 becomes KTPH001, inside an XML comment every second hyphen of a KTPH002 run becomes KTPH003 because XML forbids KTPH004 in comments, JSON strings escape backslashes and quotes, Rust doubles KTPH005 and KTPH006, Kotlin escapes KTPH007, C rewrites KTPH008 so it is not read as a trigraph, and Batch escapes KTPH009 and doubles KTPH010. Line comments and the Bash heredoc copy the picture unchanged. Three cases stay outside what escaping can fix: with a gap of 0, Bash's KTPH011 swallows a picture line that is exactly KTPH012 or KTPH013 (use the heredoc, KTPH014, or the default gap of 1); a Batch file with delayed expansion enabled still interprets KTPH015, and a KTPH016 line still expands KTPH017; and a KTPH018 comment whose last picture line ends in a backslash would swallow the next source line in C and C++, so korTTY appends an empty KTPH019 line in that case.
The KTPH000bannerKTPH001 style with the input text "Nostromo":
The dialog remembers its window position, its size, the preview zoom level, the picture sizes of the AI Picture and Image File tabs, and the copy settings between sessions.
